Alexandrian School
al-ig-ZAN-dree-uhn SKOOL
noun (church history)
From Alexandria, the great Egyptian city of learning, + school; the early Christian center of theology and interpretation associated with Clement, Origen, Athanasius, and Cyril.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Alexandrian School was the early Christian center of learning at Alexandria in Egypt, the most famous seat of scholarship in the ancient world, which shaped Christian theology for good and ill from the second through the fifth centuries. Its catechetical school produced both treasure and error. Clement of Alexandria and especially Origen pioneered Christian scholarship, textual labor, and the defense of the faith against pagan philosophy — but Origen also wove in speculations the church later condemned: the pre-existence of souls, a tendency toward universal restoration, and an allegorical method that too often loosed the text from its plain sense. Yet from the same Alexandria came mighty defenders of orthodoxy: Athanasius, who stood against the world for the deity of the Son when the whole empire went Arian, and Cyril, who at Ephesus guarded the unity of Christ's person against Nestorius. The Alexandrian tendency in Christology stressed the oneness of Christ (over against the Antiochene stress on the distinction of His natures), a stress that, pressed too far in others, slid toward the Eutychian error Chalcedon rejected. This dictionary honors Alexandria's Athanasius and Cyril as champions of the faith, while marking Origen's speculations and the school's allegorical excess as errors to be weighed and, where needful, rejected.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The early Christian school of learning at Alexandria, source of both treasure and error: Origen's scholarship and his condemned speculations; Athanasius's defense of Christ's deity and Cyril's defense of His one person; and an allegorical method that often loosed the text from its plain sense.

ALEXANDRIAN SCHOOL, noun. The early Christian center of theology and interpretation at Alexandria in Egypt.

Produced Clement and Origen — pioneers of scholarship, but Origen also of condemned speculations.

Gave the church Athanasius, defender of the Son's deity against Arianism.

Gave the church Cyril, defender of Christ's one person against Nestorius.

Marked by an allegorical method that often loosed the text from its plain sense.

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

2 Cor 4:2 — "not handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God."

2 Pet 3:16 — "in which are some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest, as they do also the other scriptures, unto their own destruction."

John 5:39 — "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Alexandrian allegorical method, when loosed from the text's plain meaning, became a fountain of error — reading hidden senses into every word and burying the literal truth; the modern heirs of that loosing are the critics and the spiritualizers who likewise make the text say whatever they please.

expand to see more

The lasting corruption of the Alexandrian School is its allegorical excess. Origen could read almost any passage as a hidden spiritual cipher, and in his hands the plain historical and grammatical sense too often vanished. With it came real heresy: the pre-existence of souls and a leaning toward the universal restoration of all things, including, in some readings, the devil himself — teachings the church later condemned. The dictionary keeps what is sound in Alexandria and rejects these speculations by name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the school's history, but its loosing of interpretation from the plain text has modern children: the critic who makes the Bible a quarry for whatever theory he brings, and the spiritualizer who finds private meanings the text never bore. The principle to recover is honest interpretation — not handling the word of God deceitfully (2 Cor 4:2), but reading it in its plain grammatical and historical sense, by which the unstable wrest the Scriptures to their own destruction (2 Pet 3:16) only when they abandon it. Athanasius and Cyril, Alexandria's glory, defended truths the text plainly teaches.

From Alexandria (the Egyptian city) + school; the early Christian seat of learning, source of Athanasius and Cyril, but also of Origen's speculation and allegorical excess.
